overview: The Khmer Empire made Angkor a major centre of power, art and water engineering in mainland Southeast Asia. Its successive capitals flourished from the ninth century onward in what is now Cambodia. The atlas’s broad outlines extend into neighbouring regions; its 900 to 1492 interval is map coverage, not precise founding and fall dates. A temple city also contained families, gardens, cooks and craftspeople.

periods.title: Early Angkorian capitals
periods.summary: The ninth century begins the sequence of Khmer capitals represented at Angkor.

periods.title: The Koh Ker capital
periods.summary: Jayavarman IV established a rival centre in 921; it became sole capital in 928.

periods.title: Angkor and royal temple building
periods.summary: Political power returned to Angkor; Suryavarman II later commissioned Angkor Wat.

periods.title: Jayavarman VII and his legacy
periods.summary: Mahayana Buddhist temple patronage and hospital foundations accompanied royal power.

periods.title: Gradual urban transformation
periods.summary: Changing land use and declining maintenance began before the traditional 1431 turning point.

periods.title: Pilgrimage and living communities
periods.summary: Angkor Wat became a major Buddhist pilgrimage destination and remains a Khmer cultural landmark.

items.text: The political centre did not always remain at Angkor. Jayavarman IV established Koh Ker in 921, first as a rival capital and then, from 928 to 944, as the empire’s sole capital. Its builders worked with enormous single blocks of stone. Royal competition helped produce striking new architecture before the court moved back to Angkor.

Suryavarman II commissioned Angkor Wat in the early twelfth century as a royal temple dedicated to Vishnu. Its galleries and towers gave religious ideas monumental form. During the sixteenth century it became an important Buddhist pilgrimage destination, drawing visitors from beyond Cambodia. The same building could acquire new sacred purposes while remaining deeply meaningful.

Jayavarman VII’s late-twelfth-century Bayon temple placed a Buddha protected by a Naga at its centre. Inscriptions in its chapels also identify gods brought together from different provinces. The temple linked royal authority with a wider sacred landscape. Its famous tower faces remain debated rather than securely identified portraits of one person.

The Elephant Terrace was a platform for royal pavilions, about 300 metres long. Large postholes help reveal wooden buildings that have disappeared. The Chinese visitor Zhou Daguan reported that the king appeared at a golden window to hear complaints and give judgments in the late thirteenth century. Government could be a very public performance.

Excavations inside Angkor Wat’s enclosure found traces of twelfth-century households: postholes, flat stones, pottery and cooking features. The archaeologists could not reconstruct a complete house, but these remains show people living around the sacred monument. Families left a quieter archaeological record than kings, sometimes just a cooking place and broken dishes.

Cooking in the temple enclosure used both portable ceramic stoves and hearths built at ground level. Rice husks and the bases of rice grains show processing on site. Plants associated with domestic gardening included bananas, palms and pepper. Preparing supper involved growing, cleaning and processing ingredients before anything reached the pot.

Charred cotton seeds from the Angkor Wat households probably relate to textile production. Residents may have grown cotton for exchange or processed it at home. This is a useful reminder that household work could produce clothing materials as well as meals. The seeds survive because some were burned, accidentally preserving a trace of an ordinary industry.

Bayon’s carved scenes include small market stalls, workers laying out a road and women preparing fish on skewers. These are artistic images, but their specific tasks bring working people into view alongside rulers and gods. Even a magnificent capital needed somebody to prepare dinner; the stone fish, unfortunately, are no longer accepting orders.

Angkor’s canals, catchments and embankments formed a connected water system built up over centuries. A modern network study showed how long drought followed by unusually wet years could destabilize it. Water engineering was a major achievement, but keeping old channels working required maintenance. Researchers still debate how environmental stress and political changes interacted.

sections.title: Healthcare, learning and a written voice

items.text: The Say Fong hospital inscription of 1186 describes two physicians and other staff. Its instructions assign cooks duties involving water, fuel and cleaning the temple, while women pound rice. Healthcare depended on feeding people and maintaining the institution as well as the work of doctors.

The same hospital text lists rice for patients and supplies such as honey, sesame, ginger and cardamom. It promises treatment across the four social categories named in the inscription and asks future rulers to protect the foundation. These are royal provisions and aspirations, not proof that every patient received the same care or that every remedy worked.

Queen Indradevi composed a Sanskrit poem carved on the great stele of Phimeanakas around 1190 to 1200. It honoured her deceased sister Jayarajadevi and their husband, Jayavarman VII. Its final verses celebrate learning and her own composition. A woman at court could be an accomplished author and patron; this does not tell us how widely ordinary girls attended school.

A hospital stele east of Ta Keo, dated 1108 in the Saka calendar, or 1186 CE, opens “namo vuddhāya”, meaning “Homage to the Buddha”. This is the editor’s Roman-letter transcription of Sanskrit originally carved in Khmer script. The brief greeting belongs to a Buddhist hospital foundation, linking written royal patronage with concern for illness.

Mud from Angkor Thom’s moat preserves a history of its surroundings. Researchers found less evidence of burning, erosion and forest disturbance from the early fourteenth century. By that century’s end, floating vegetation suggests the moat was no longer maintained. This supports a gradual reduction of activity in the administrative centre, long before the familiar 1431 collapse story.

Angkor is still an inhabited landscape. UNESCO describes villages, rice farming, weaving, palm-sugar production and ceremonies at temple sites. These are living Khmer communities, not actors filling an empty ruin. Modern practices need their own dates and histories, but their presence makes clear that the disappearance of imperial power did not mean the disappearance of Khmer people.

ending.text: Angkor’s role as an imperial centre diminished through a long transformation involving changing settlement, water management and regional conflict. The traditional 1431 Ayutthayan attack does not explain all the archaeological changes. Angkor Wat later flourished as a Buddhist pilgrimage site, and Khmer communities continued. The atlas endpoint of 1492 is not a documented moment when this people or its culture ended.
